Q: How to use isinstance on functools.cache cached classes? A:

We can preserve the initial class like this:

import functools
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PersonBase:
    name: str = "John Doe"
    age: int = 30

Person = functools.cache(PersonBase)

Of course, if anyone use the PersonBase to get instances, it won't use the cache and it won't be singletons.

>>> p = Person()
>>> isinstance(p, PersonBase)
True

Q: Casting an out-of-range counter through DOUBLE clamps it to INT64 max A:

Well, Apache IoTDB is built on Java, and under the Java Language Specification, when you convert a double to a long, and that value happens to exceed the maximum allowed value, then Java, being Java, just caps the value at Long.MAX_VALUE (the value you're seeing).

Regarding your 2 questions:

  1. Yes, it does.

  2. No, IoTDB can't override the JVM's default saturation behavior.

You have 2 solutions:

  1. Keep the direct conversion, since it uses string parsing methods (e.g., Long.parseLong), it will check the bounds and throw an error when a number is too large.

  2. Add a guard before conversion.

Q: Sikuli: for loop/if else statement not working correctly A:

Are you trying to do this in sikuli-IDE? The issue there is that there is not always a good traceback provided.

In your second example you seem to be skipping an index entirely probably because the caption is not found so nothing executes and it jumps to the next iteration. This is skipping the iteration with no output since all of the code is within the if block that re-checks for something that was already determined as existing.

I think the issue in the first part is you are not finding the match and then failing at the click() call (and the traceback doesn't end up helping). exists() returns a match, and also sets the value for getLastMatch(). You could try either setting a local variable with the match returned by exists() or in the else clause using getLastMatch().click() to click that region that was found (presumably your "caption.png").

You could also try specifying a wait time in the exists() line.

Lastly you could try setting each image as a pattern and use the similarity to pare the results down to one single match.

It is hard to give a definitive answer without a screen shot or info about what is on the screen and how many of the image could be on the screen. I can't comment yet, but if you could provide more information I can edit this answer to include a more specific answer.

Q: websocket always triggers onerror(undefined) with Chrome, but not with Firefox A:

Guys.

Here is my experience about the issue. Yesterday, my php simple chatting socket script worked well in both of firefox and chrome. Suddenly it did not work in chrome today. Not sure why? But after the request header value was printed, I found that the header length was longer than 1024 byte. (I tested by getting 1024 byte in server.php under a domain without login). Maybe after I logged into the domain, cache length was added into the http request header.

I increased the length value for socket_read function to 5120 byte before performed handshaking. It was enough value to get full request header. My problem was solved since server.php handshaking function could validate sec-websocket-key from request header.

Hope other guys to take care of websocket request header length.

Regards, Yin

Q: sql query to show results vertically A:

You can use a static PIVOT if you only are going to have a few columns but I am guessing that you will have more than 2 IDs so you will probably want to use a Dynamic PIVOT for this query. Using a dynamic pivot will allow you to have more than the two ids you provided, it will grab all of the Ids from the table and then PIVOT:

create table temp
(
    id int,
    name varchar(10),
    description varchar(20)
)

insert into temp values (1, 'Test1a', 'TestDesc1a')
insert into temp values (1, 'Test1b', 'TestDesc1b')
insert into temp values (2, 'Test2a', 'TestDesc2a')
insert into temp values (2, 'Test2b', 'TestDesc2b')


DECLARE @cols AS NVARCHAR(MAX),
    @query  AS NVARCHAR(MAX);

SET @cols = STUFF((SELECT distinct ',' + QUOTENAME(c.id) 
            FROM temp c
            FOR XML PATH(''), TYPE
            ).value('.', 'NVARCHAR(MAX)') 
        ,1,1,'')

set @query = 'SELECT ''Name'' as [Column], ' + @cols + ' from 
            (
                select id
                    , name
                from temp
           ) x
            pivot 
            (
                 max(name)
                for id in (' + @cols + ')
            ) p 
            UNION 
            SELECT ''Description'' as [Column], ' + @cols + ' from 
            (
                select id
                    , description
                from temp
           ) x
            pivot 
            (
                 max(description)
                for id in (' + @cols + ')
            ) p '


execute(@query)

drop table temp

Results:

Column          1             2
Description     TestDesc1b    TestDesc2b
Name            Test1b        Test2b

Q: Memoization In Python A:

Note: I won't talk about the function itself, how to optimize it, how to fix it, etc. Answers already explains what is does, without addressing what it is and what it means.

I'll try to answer the exact question OP had.

This is a code I saw for avaluating fibonacci number using memoization, what does [0,1]+[-1]*(n-1) mean? Can you please explain me what does this type of writing represent?

[0,1]+[-1]*(n-1) is specifically a way to pre-allocate the list your function needs to create, instead of increasing its size when adding new elements everytime it computes a new one as this function would:

def fib_mem(n, result = None):
    if result is None:
        result = [0, 1]
    if len(result) < n+2:
        fib_mem(n-1, result)
        result.append(result[-1] + result[-2])
    return result[n]

That's all. You don't need it to memoïze the fib computation, as the function I just showed do use memoïzation and compute fib(1000) almost instantly, but it helps reducing the memory reallocation of the list.

[0,1]+[-1]*(n-1) could have been [0,1]+[None]*(n-1), [0,1]+["yolo"]*(n-1) or anything, as it's sole purpose is to make the list the desired size from the start. Its content doesn't matter (except the first two values of course) when it is initialized.

Q: c++ buffering. help me please A:

std::cin and std::cout have separate buffers. When you do std::cout << y << std::endl;, that flushes the buffer for std::cout, but has no effect on the buffer for std::cin.

There is a similar situation that can be a little deceptive. The buffers for std::cout and std::cin are linked together to an extent. When you try to read something from std::cin, that will flush anything in the std::cout buffer before it tries to read from std::cin, to assure that if you print out a prompt, the user will see it before they need to enter the input data. But that's a one-way street: reading from std::cin flushes the std::cout buffer, but things you do with std::cout don't affect the buffer for std::cin.
